title: The Dangerous Appeal of Fake AI Users
intro: AI-generated "synthetic users" look like research but aren't. LLMs predict words, not behavior. The things that make real research valuable — confusion, workarounds, surprise — are exactly what AI can't produce.

learn.title: Why synthetic users fail
learn.text:
Some teams prompt LLMs with persona data and treat the output as user research. The fundamental problem:

**LLMs predict the most likely next words.** They don't generate insight — they generate plausibility.

The output mirrors your assumptions right back at you. You describe your persona in the prompt, the model produces responses consistent with that description, and you call it "validation."

That's not research. That's an expensive mirror.

Real users give you data you didn't expect. Synthetic users give you data you already assumed.

left.label: Real user
items: Uses a workaround because the system is slow
Clicks by mistake and stays quiet
Doesn't notice a feature until pointed out

try.q: You prompt an LLM with a persona and ask it to 'use' your prototype. What are you actually getting?
options: Responses consistent with your own assumptions in the prompt
Genuine user behavior data
Statistically valid feedback
An unbiased perspective
try.explain: The model mirrors what you put in. Your assumptions go in, your assumptions come back out — dressed up as user quotes.

learn.title: The surprise IS the value
learn.text:
The most important moments in user research are the ones you didn't predict:

• A user avoids a button they don't understand
• Someone lies in a survey to finish faster
• A participant feels embarrassed to ask a question
• A user believes a task worked when it actually didn't
• Someone asks a coworker instead of using the feature

These are **unknown unknowns** — and they're where the biggest product decisions come from.

An LLM has no lived experience. It doesn't pause, get confused, feel frustrated, or choose the wrong path. It can't reveal those moments because it never has them.

Real research deliberately slows you down. That's a feature, not a bug — you get fewer answers, but they're the ones that matter.

try.q: Why can't AI replicate the most valuable moments in UX research?
options: AI has no lived experience — it can't get confused, frustrated, or surprised
AI is too slow to process user tasks
AI doesn't have access to the right data
AI can only process text, not visuals
try.explain: Real insight comes from moments of genuine human confusion, emotion, and workaround — things that require lived experience, not word prediction.

learn.title: How we got here
learn.text:
Synthetic users are a symptom, not the root cause. The real problem:

**PM-led research without methods training.** Product managers took on research but shifted from observation to conversation, from evidence to opinion. Short, frequent "customer touchpoints" give the appearance of learning without the depth.

**Speed valued over rigor.** The claim that experienced teams can move fast without sacrificing quality falls apart — most teams aren't experienced, and they cut corners.

**The illusion of rigor.** AI output comes with transcripts, quotes, and takeaways that look real. People without research training can't tell the difference.

**Once adopted, hard to abandon.** Teams get detached from the people they build for. AI makes poor practices cheap and repeatable, which institutionalizes bad research at scale.

The author doesn't reject AI in product development — only its use as a replacement for actual users.

try.q: A PM says: "We ran 50 synthetic user sessions this week — way more than we could do with real users." What's the problem?
options: Volume of bad data doesn't produce insight — it produces false confidence
50 sessions is too few
Synthetic users are fine but should be combined with surveys
The PM should have used a better prompt
try.explain: Scaling bad methodology doesn't make it good. Cheaper and faster doesn't matter if the data can't tell you what you need to know.

test.q: What is the fundamental flaw of using LLMs as synthetic users?
options: LLMs predict likely words, not actual user behavior
LLMs are too expensive for research
LLMs can only handle text, not visual designs
LLMs require too much setup time
test.explain: LLMs are word-prediction machines. They produce plausible-sounding responses, not behavioral data. That's a category error.

test.q: Which of these can a real user do but a synthetic user cannot?
options: Give up out of frustration and use a workaround
Answer questions about their preferences
Describe what they would do in a scenario
Evaluate the visual appeal of a design
test.explain: Real frustration, real workarounds, and real emotional responses require lived experience — exactly what LLMs lack.

test.q: Why does the article call surprise 'the value' of real research?
options: Unknown unknowns drive the biggest product decisions
Surprises make research reports more interesting
Users enjoy being surprised during testing
Unexpected findings generate more stakeholder attention
test.explain: The moments you didn't predict — confusion, workarounds, misunderstandings — are where the most important insights come from.

test.q: According to the article, why is it hard for teams to stop using synthetic users once adopted?
options: Teams get detached from real users and AI makes poor practices cheap to scale
The technology is too integrated into their tools
Synthetic users produce better results over time
Management mandates their continued use
test.explain: Once teams stop observing real people, they lose connection to actual user behavior. AI makes it easy to keep going — poor research at scale.

test.q: Does the author reject all use of AI in product development?
options: No — only its use as a replacement for real users
Yes — AI has no place in product work
Yes — AI introduces too many biases
No — but only if used by trained researchers
test.explain: The article specifically says AI has value in product development — just not as a substitute for observing real human behavior.
